Temperature Measurement
Liquid in Glass Thermometer Working Principle, Construction, Immersion Types and Emergent Stem Correction

A glass thermometer looks simple, but dip it to the wrong depth and the reading can be off by more than a degree. We go through the bulb, capillary and scale, then correct the emergent stem with a worked example.

Bulb and capillary Mercury vs spirit Immersion types Stem correction Calibration

Glass stem thermometers are still used in labs and plants, and reading one correctly depends on how it is built, what liquid it holds, how deep it is immersed and how it was calibrated. The emergent stem correction formula is worked through with a calculator and a solved example.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a liquid in glass thermometer works, how to read it correctly and how to apply the emergent stem correction.
Quick Answer

What is a liquid in glass thermometer and how does it work?

Liquid in glass thermometer readings come from thermal expansion: mercury or alcohol sealed in a glass bulb expands more than the glass and climbs a fine capillary against a scale. If part of the column sits outside the bath, add the stem correction K × n × (t1 minus t2). For mercury with n = 70 and a 60 °C difference, that is 0.672 °C.

What Is a Liquid in Glass Thermometer?

A liquid in glass thermometer is a direct reading temperature instrument in which a liquid sealed inside a glass bulb expands into a narrow capillary tube and the length of the column is read against a scale. It needs no power, no wiring and no electronics, which is why labs still use it as a working reference.

Key Facts
  • Principle: the liquid expands more than the glass, so the column rises with temperature
  • Mercury freezes near minus 38.8 °C, which sets its low limit
  • Three immersion types: total, partial (often 76 mm) and complete
  • Stem correction = K × n × (t1 minus t2), K about 0.00016 for mercury

You will find this instrument in QC labs, boiler houses, cold rooms and teaching labs across India. If you are new to the wider family, start with our overview of industrial temperature sensor types.

Like every thermometer, it relies on the zeroth law of thermodynamics: the bulb and the process reach the same temperature after enough time. That is why a cold thermometer dipped quickly into hot oil gives a low first reading.

Do You Know?

Wikipedia records that Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit began making mercury thermometers around 1713 and was selling them by 1717.

Advertisement

How Does a Liquid in Glass Thermometer Work?

It works on differential thermal expansion: the liquid in the bulb expands far more than the glass around it, so the extra volume has only one place to go, up the capillary. Because the bore is very fine, a tiny volume change becomes a long, easily read movement of the column.

The bulb holds most of the liquid, so its size and wall thickness decide sensitivity and speed. A thin walled bulb settles faster, a trade off we also discuss in sensor response time.

Bulb
Thin glass reservoir that holds most of the liquid.
Capillary bore
Fine, uniform tube inside the stem where the column moves.
Stem
Thick glass rod that protects the bore and magnifies the column.
Scale
Graduations etched on the stem or printed on a card.
Contraction chamber
Bore enlargement that shortens the stem or stops the column falling into the bulb.
Expansion chamber
Top enlargement, at least equal to 20 mm of capillary, that limits pressure.

The part descriptions follow NBS Monograph 150 by Jacquelyn Wise. NBS adds that total immersion thermometers graduated above 150 °C must be gas filled, normally with dry nitrogen, to stop the mercury distilling and the column separating.

Mercury vs Alcohol Thermometer: Which Liquid Is Better?

Mercury is better for accuracy and higher temperatures, while alcohol and other organic liquids are better for low temperatures and wherever mercury is restricted. The ranges below come from Wikipedia and the K values from NBS.

Fill liquidUseful rangeK valueNotes
MercuryAbout minus 37 to 356 °C0.00016Opaque, does not wet glass, toxic
Mercury with nitrogen in quartzUp to about 800 °C0.00016Special high range designs
Mercury thalliumDown to about minus 56 °CSimilar to mercuryExtends the low end
Alcohol, toluene (spirit)Below the mercury limit0.001Dyed red or blue, wets the glass
GalinstanMercury free optionMaker dataGallium, indium and tin alloy

The organic liquid K is about six times the mercury value, so stem errors grow much faster with a spirit fill.

Quick Tip

Read a mercury column at the top of its convex meniscus and a spirit column at the bottom of its concave meniscus. Keep your eye level with the meniscus to avoid parallax.

Compared with a bimetallic dial thermometer or a gas filled thermometer, the glass design reads finer but is less rugged and cannot send a remote signal.

What Are Total, Partial and Complete Immersion Thermometers?

The immersion type tells you how much of the thermometer must be inside the measured medium for the scale to read correctly. NBS Monograph 150 defines three types.

Total immersion

Reads correctly when the bulb and the whole liquid column are at the measured temperature.

Best for: Calibration baths and reference work
Most accurate
Partial immersion

Reads correctly when the bulb and a fixed stem length, marked by a line such as 76 mm, are immersed.

Best for: Process and routine lab use
Most common
Complete immersion

Reads correctly only when the entire thermometer, including the expansion chamber, is at the measured temperature.

Best for: Freezers and special chambers
Rare

NBS notes that partial immersion accuracy of 0.1 to 0.3 °C in the 0 to 100 °C range is possible only if the emergent stem temperature is known. In a plant room at 35 °C, check which stem temperature the certificate assumed.

Advertisement

How to Calculate Emergent Stem Correction

Multiply the coefficient K by the number of emergent degrees n and by the difference between the bulb temperature t1 and the mean stem temperature t2. Add the result to the observed reading.

Correction = K × n × (t1 minus t2)
K = 0.00016 for mercury in glass (°C)
K = 0.001 for organic liquids (°C)
n = reading minus bath surface mark
True temperature = t1 + correction

NBS gives K for mercury in normal glass as about 0.000158 at 0 °C rising to 0.000183 at 400 °C, and accepts 0.00016 when the glass type is unknown. ICL Calibration Laboratories lists 0.00009 for Fahrenheit mercury scales, so match K to the scale unit.

Solved example: a total immersion mercury thermometer reads 90 °C with the bath surface at the 20 °C mark, so n is 70. An auxiliary thermometer halfway up the emergent column reads 30 °C.

n = 90 minus 20 = 70
Correction = 0.00016 × 70 × (90 minus 30)
= 0.00016 × 70 × 60
= 0.672 °C
True temperature = 90 + 0.672 = 90.67 °C

With a spirit fill and the same numbers, the correction becomes 0.001 × 70 × 60 = 4.2 °C. NBS warns that the correction can reach 20 degrees when the emergent column is long and the temperature difference is large.

Emergent Stem Correction Calculator
Result
Correction 0.672 °C, true temperature 90.67 °C

ICL points out that the stem temperature is hard to measure precisely. Put its uncertainty in your measurement uncertainty budget.

How to Calibrate a Liquid in Glass Thermometer Against a Reference

You calibrate it by comparison in a stirred bath against a reference thermometer with a traceable certificate, reading both at several points and then confirming the ice point. The steps follow the NBS comparison method.

1
Inspect
Look for separated columns, gas bubbles, cracks and faded scale lines.
2
Ice point
Read the thermometer in an ice bath of shaved ice and pure water.
3
Immerse
Place it at its marked immersion depth next to the reference probe.
4
Stabilise
Wait until both readings stop moving, then tap lightly before reading.
5
Record
Read test and reference values at three to five points up the scale.
6
Correct
Write the correction at each point and the ice point on the certificate.

NBS advises reading the ice point after the thermometer has rested at least 3 days near 23 °C, and a careful ice point can be realised to better than 0.01 °C. Once calibrated, an ice point check alone confirms the calibration if the instrument has not been abused.

For the reference side you can use a dry block calibrator with a liquid insert or a stirred bath. The chain back to national standards is covered in our calibration traceability guide.

PDF
NBS Monograph 150: Liquid in Glass Thermometry
J. A. Wise, National Bureau of Standards, 1976. Construction, immersion, stem correction and calibration.

What Causes Errors in a Glass Thermometer?

Most errors come from wrong immersion, separated columns, parallax, slow response and ice point drift. Follow the flowchart before every important reading.

SymptomLikely causeField fix
Reading low in a hot bathEmergent stem cooler than bulbImmerse to the mark or apply the stem correction
Gap in the columnColumn separation after a knockCool the bulb gently to rejoin, then recheck the ice point
Ice point shiftedGlass ageing or overheatingRecord the new ice point and shift all corrections
Different readings by two peopleParallax at the meniscusRead with the eye level to the column top

NBS also observes that horizontal use may raise a reading by a few hundredths of a degree. For causes across all sensors, see temperature measurement errors.

Myth: A glass thermometer never needs calibration because it has no electronics.
Fact: The bulb slowly changes volume with age and heating, so the ice point moves.
Myth: Immersion depth does not change the reading.
Fact: A long cool emergent stem can make the reading low by more than a degree.
Myth: Spirit thermometers are as accurate as mercury ones.
Fact: Spirit liquids wet the glass and have a K about six times larger.
Advertisement

Advantages and Limitations of Glass Stem Thermometers

You get a cheap, stable, power free reading with fine resolution. The price is fragile glass and a reading you can only see on the spot.

Advantages
  • Needs no power supply or wiring
  • Fine resolution on precision types
  • Good long term stability with care
  • Low cost and easy ice point check
Limitations
  • Glass breaks easily and mercury is toxic
  • No remote output for DCS or PLC logging
  • Slow response with thick bulbs
  • Accuracy depends on immersion depth

For a 4 to 20 mA loop, an RTD sensor in a thermowell is the usual replacement.

Do You Know?

The European Union restricted mercury in measuring devices under Directive 2007/51/EC from 3 April 2009, as Wikipedia notes. ASTM E2251 now specifies ASTM pattern thermometers with low hazard precision liquids as replacements.

Where Is a Liquid in Glass Thermometer Still Used?

Laboratories, standard test methods and local spot checks still use it wherever they need a cheap, independent reference that runs without power.

Petroleum test methods
ASTM pattern thermometers for flash point, viscosity and distillation tests.
QC and pharma labs
Water baths and incubators needing an independent check.
Cold chain
Spirit types in refrigerators and cold rooms for daily logs.

ASTM E1 covers the specification of ASTM glass thermometers, ASTM E77 their inspection and verification, and ISO 386 the design, construction and use of laboratory types. For Fahrenheit pattern readings, a temperature unit converter saves time.

  • Confirm the immersion type and depth marked on the stem
  • Check the column for gaps and bubbles
  • Verify the ice point against the certificate
  • Apply K for the right liquid and scale unit

Quick Tip

Before you trust an old lab thermometer, hold it against a light and scan the whole column for small gaps. A separated column is the most common hidden fault.

Liquid in Glass Thermometer FAQ

What is the working principle of a liquid in glass thermometer in simple words?

It works because the liquid in the bulb expands more than the glass as temperature rises. The extra liquid climbs a fine capillary, and you read the column height on the scale, roughly 0.016 percent volume change per degree for mercury relative to glass.

What is the difference between total and partial immersion thermometers with example?

A total immersion thermometer must have its whole liquid column in the bath, while a partial immersion type is dipped only to a marked line such as 76 mm. Using a total immersion unit at 76 mm depth needs a stem correction to read correctly.

How to calculate emergent stem correction for a mercury thermometer step by step?

Find n as the reading minus the scale mark at the bath surface, then measure the mean stem temperature t2. Multiply 0.00016 by n and by t1 minus t2, so 70 degrees and a 60 °C difference give 0.672, added to the reading.

Which is better for low temperature measurement, mercury or alcohol thermometer?

Alcohol and other organic liquids are better below about minus 38 °C because mercury freezes there. Mercury is the better choice above room temperature, where its smaller K value of 0.00016 and clean meniscus give lower uncertainty than spirit fills.

Why does a liquid in glass thermometer show a gap in the column?

A gap usually means column separation caused by a knock, rapid cooling or shipping vibration. You can often rejoin it by gently cooling the bulb so the mercury retreats into it, then you must recheck the ice point before using it again.

How often should a liquid in glass thermometer be calibrated or checked?

A full multipoint calibration is normally done when the thermometer is new and after damage or overheating. Between full calibrations, NBS advises that an ice point check confirms the calibration, so set a regular ice point check interval in your quality system.

What We Learn Today

  • A liquid in glass thermometer works because the liquid expands more than the glass, pushing a column up a fine capillary against a scale.
  • Total, partial and complete immersion types each read correctly only at their own depth, so always check the mark on the stem first.
  • Emergent stem correction equals K times n times t1 minus t2, with K about 0.00016 for mercury and 0.001 for organic liquids.
